passage: Week one. Karthik lay awake till three, running through it: what if he failed chemistry, what if the headache meant something serious, what if his friends were laughing at him in the group chat. At breakfast, when his sister Ganga asked for the salt, he snapped at her. Week four. It hadn't stopped. He'd dropped cricket practice because his mind wouldn't sit still long enough to bat. Ganga found him at midnight on the balcony, jaw tight. "It's every night, isn't it?" He nodded. Week five. Ganga walked with him to the school counsellor's room. "I'll wait outside," she said. Inside, Karthik said it out loud for the first time: "I can't stop the what-ifs." The counsellor listened, then said, "Thank you for telling me. Let's work on this together."

qa.q: What did Karthik drop because his mind wouldn't sit still?
What was Karthik worried about at night in week one?
qa.a: He worried he would fail chemistry, that his headache meant something serious, and that his friends were laughing at him.

qa.q: What turning point came in week five?
qa.a: With Ganga's support, Karthik went to the school counsellor and said the worries out loud for the first time.

qa.q: How might Ganga have felt when Karthik snapped at her?
qa.a: She may have felt hurt at first, but later saw it was part of how tense and sleepless he was.

grounding: It shows a teenager who is tense, sleepless and irritable from constant what-ifs that last and limit his life, and who talks to a counsellor.

passage: "Ojas, you think Bhavna Bua was always this calm? Sit down. When I was sixteen, I couldn't sleep for months. Every night my head ran in circles. What if I fail? What if this cough is something bad? What if my friends secretly hate me? I stopped going to badminton. I snapped at your father, poor boy, over nothing. Everyone said, 'She's just moody. Teenagers.' But it wasn't just moodiness. It went on and on, and my world was getting smaller. My English teacher noticed I'd stopped smiling. She took me to the school counsellor. I was embarrassed. But talking to her, week after week, taught me to catch the what-ifs before they ran away with me. So if your head won't stop at night, beta, don't wait. Tell me. We'll find someone to talk to."

qa.q: What sport did Bhavna Bua stop going to?
How did Bhavna feel about going to the counsellor at first?
What was the turning point for young Bhavna, and why did it help?
qa.a: Her English teacher noticed she had stopped smiling and took her to the school counsellor; talking there week after week taught her to catch the what-ifs.

qa.q: How might the people who called Bhavna 'just moody' have seen her differently?
qa.a: If they had understood, they would have seen a teenager struggling with anxiety that lasted and limited her life, not simple moodiness.

grounding: An aunt recalls her own teenage years of sleeplessness and constant what-ifs that lasted and limited her life, and how talking to a counsellor helped.
